archetype.name: Rebuilding (goalie-propped)
archetype.definition: A team still well short of NHL-average play at 5-on-5. Its goaltenders are keeping a lopsided shot and chance gap from turning into a worse record, while a cold-shooting forward group and a thin blue line leave Macklin Celebrini doing most of the lifting.

report.headline: Good goaltending, bad everything else: the Sharks have slid back toward 2024-25
report.take:
San Jose sits 7-11-1, seventh in the Pacific and 28th of 32 on the site. The record is not the alarming part. The play under it is. The Sharks own 43.2% of the 5-on-5 expected goals (29th) and 47% of the shot attempts (27th), and they give up 29.8 shots a game, 28th in the league. That expected-goals share is worse than last season's 47.6% and right back where the 20-50-12 team of 2024-25 sat at 43.7%. Last year's 86-point jump also leaned on 6.1 standings points beyond what its goal differential implied. This year that cushion is basically gone at 0.5, so the record now tells the truth about a team losing by 1.11 goals a game.

The one group holding up its end is in net. The team's goalies are +7.3 goals saved above expected, fifth in the league and graded A-. That is a reversal from last season's -25.7. The save percentage (.889, 17th) looks merely average, but the gap between it and the GSAx tells the real story. Askarov and Nedeljkovic are facing a heavy diet of quality chances and still stopping more than an average goalie would. Both are positive on the season, with Nedeljkovic at +5.1 in seven starts.

The skaters are the problem, graded D- up front and D on the back end. Celebrini is the exception. He has 21 points in 17 games, 10 on the power play, and a 51.1% expected-goals share, the only regular forward on the right side of even. Everyone else is under water, several badly: Misa at 39%, Stenberg at 39.9%, Orlov at 39.4% with a -12. Opponents' forwards score 0.91 points a game more against San Jose than their own averages predict, 26th in the league, with wingers doing the most damage.

The skid is real but partly exaggerated. The Sharks are 0-5 in their last five, outscored 22-8, and 0-4 in November on 1.75 goals a game. Some of that is finishing that should recover. Their 9.2% all-situations shooting is 30th against a league average of 11.6%, and the 5-on-5 PDO of 96.2 is well below where teams settle. Expect more goals. Don't expect a different team: the shot and chance deficits are structural, and they are what history says this roster is.

strengths.title: Goaltending saving them from worse
strengths.body: San Jose's goalies rank fifth in goals saved above expected despite a middling save percentage, which means they are facing tough chances and beating them. Both starters are positive, so this is not a one-man hot streak. Some regression is possible over 63 more games, but this tandem has earned its A-, a sharp turn from last year's league-worst-type number.

strengths.title: Celebrini drives everything that works
strengths.body: Celebrini logs 23 minutes a night, sits 25th of 233 centers on the site, and has 21 points in 17 games. He is the only regular forward with a positive expected-goals share. Half his points come on the power play, which is why a 21.4% unit can be roughly league-average despite a weak supporting cast.

concerns.title: Badly outplayed at 5-on-5
concerns.body: A 43.2% expected-goals share and nearly 30 shots against a game put San Jose among the league's worst process teams. This is a step back from last season and level with the 2024-25 basement team, so it reads as the roster's true talent, not a slump. Nothing in the depth chart suggests it fixes itself.

concerns.title: Depth skaters getting buried
concerns.body: Beyond Celebrini, the forward group grades D- and the defense D. Big-minute pieces like Nurse (41.5% xGF, two points in 21 minutes a night) and Orlov (39.4%, -12) are losing their shifts. Opposing forwards beat their expected scoring against this team by one of the widest margins in the league.

concerns.title: Finishing has dried up
concerns.body: The skaters are converting 9.2% of their shots, 30th, while getting a near-average volume of shots on goal. That part should bounce back some. But November's 1.75 goals a game is also what happens when chance quality is this poor, so the rebound has a ceiling.

trend.note: October was competitive at 7-8 despite poor shot numbers. November has opened 0-4, part of a five-game losing streak in which the Sharks were outscored 22-8.

weekAhead.headline: Three home games, but every opponent ranks above them
weekAhead.body:
The week opens with three of four at home: the Islanders, Penguins and Predators, with a trip to Utah in between. The Islanders and Predators are tough matchups for a slumping offense. Both have top-six goaltending by GSAx and top-five penalty kills, and Nashville's defense holds opposing wingers furthest under their norms of almost anyone. Those games project as low-scoring, which favors San Jose's goalies but not its 9.2% shooting.

The softer spots are Pittsburgh and Utah, and for the same reason: shaky goaltending. Pittsburgh's .876 save percentage is 28th, and its forwards give up the third-most points over expectation in the league. That is the likeliest place for the Sharks' shooters to break out. Utah's goalies are 31st in GSAx, but the Mammoth have the league's second-best expected-goals share and an A-graded skating group, so the Sharks will be chasing the puck all night. A split is a fair outcome. Extending the streak to eight or nine is a real risk.

keyMatchups.title: Pittsburgh's leaky net
keyMatchups.body: The Penguins out-attempt opponents at 53% but stop only .876 of shots, and they sit 31st in points versus goal differential. Their forwards allow the third-most points over expectation in the league. This is the week's best chance for San Jose's cold shooters to cash in.

keyMatchups.title: Utah's special teams mismatch
keyMatchups.body: Utah's power play converts at 37.1%, second in the league, against a Sharks penalty kill of 76.5%. The Mammoth's own kill is just 69.6%, 27th, which gives Celebrini's power-play unit a real opening. Penalty discipline in Salt Lake may decide it.

keyMatchups.title: Stingy goalies on the Island
keyMatchups.body: The Islanders are fourth in GSAx and fifth in save percentage, and their penalty kill is fifth. Nashville is sixth in GSAx with the third-best kill. San Jose's goaltending advantage disappears in these two games.

weekAhead.watch: Whether the forwards finally finish against Pittsburgh's and Utah's weak goaltending. If they can't score there, the shooting slump is less bad luck than bad chances.

restOfSeason.body:
The 82-game pace is 30 wins and 65 standings points, and that is about right for this team. Shooting should climb from 30th toward something more normal, which adds goals. That is roughly offset by the risk that a goaltending tandem saving goals at a top-five clip drifts back toward average while still facing nearly 30 shots a night. With no close-game luck baked into the record this time, there is little to regress downward in the standings and little reason to expect a surge. I project 26 to 32 wins and 60 to 72 points, with scoring recovering into the 2.6 to 2.9 goals a game range.

The real gauge is development, not the standings. Celebrini is already a top-line driver, but the rest of the lineup is losing its minutes badly. Unless the depth skaters' expected-goals shares move toward 45% and beyond, this looks like a bottom-five finish that undoes some of last season's 86-point optimism. A playoff push is not on the table.
swingFactors: Whether the goalies keep saving goals above expected
Depth forwards and defense closing the 5-on-5 gap

confidence.note: Only 19 games, but the shot and chance numbers match the team's recent history.
